subtitle: Learn to recognize concerns about work, respond appropriately to requests and connect people with support. Throughout, you will protect each person’s dignity and privacy.
scope: For supervisors building a basic understanding of mental health and workplace support. This course does not diagnose a condition, provide treatment, determine leave eligibility, assess a direct threat, or replace agency emergency procedures. Use HR, the ADA Coordinator, Employee Assistance Program resources, and other responsible offices as appropriate. Personal disclosure is not required for participation.
introTranscript: Mental health can affect work, and workplace experiences can affect wellbeing. Supervisors need a clear response that stays within their role. This course follows practice situations involving a work concern, a request connected to a health condition, coworkers’ questions, a referral, and follow-through. It separates ordinary supervision, an accommodation process, leave questions, professional support, and urgent safety response. Leaders practice responding respectfully without assuming that a diagnosis predicts ability or safety. The goal is practical coordination: clear expectations, usable information, appropriate support routes, and decisions based on relevant evidence.

intro.heading: Describe work concerns without diagnosing a person
intro.body:
A supervisor may notice missed deadlines, withdrawal from a meeting, or a change in work quality. Those observations deserve attention, but do not identify a mental health condition. Several explanations are possible, including unclear priorities, a difficult workload, an unresolved support need, or events outside work. A respectful conversation begins with what is known.

In a practice benefits team, an employee misses two agreed review dates. The supervisor can describe those dates and their effect on the team. Calling the employee depressed, unstable, or uncommitted adds an unsupported conclusion. Even if a condition is known, it does not by itself establish inability to perform a job or a safety risk.

Speak privately, explain the work expectation, and invite discussion of work barriers or support. The supervisor’s role is not to obtain a diagnosis or provide therapy. If information raises a possible accommodation, leave, complaint, or urgent safety issue, use the appropriate process rather than treating the conversation as an informal assessment.

flashcards.back: A health condition that may affect a person’s thoughts, emotions, behavior, or daily functioning; a supervisor does not diagnose it.
A description of what occurred in the work, separated from an assumed medical explanation.
A communication that a work change is needed because of a medical condition; special legal wording is not required.
A support resource for personal or work-related concerns. A referral does not replace an accommodation, leave, or complaint process.
Limits on who receives personal information and for what authorized purpose; do not promise secrecy beyond applicable responsibilities.
Use of established emergency or crisis routes when immediate help is needed, rather than routine email or a course activity.

items.title: Observation
items.body: A useful observation is specific enough to review: two scheduled reviews were not completed by the agreed dates. It explains the work effect without claiming a cause. This gives the employee room to clarify priorities, conditions, or support needs instead of defending against a personal label.

items.title: Stereotype
items.body: A known or presumed mental health condition does not establish dangerousness, incompetence, or lack of commitment. In the benefits-team case, replacing work evidence with a stereotype can distort both feedback and future assignments. Relevant concerns need their proper evidence and authorized review, not a diagnosis-based prediction.

items.title: Opening
items.body: Start with the observed work and an invitation to discuss what affects it: identify the dates, explain the needed review, and ask what barriers should be addressed. Do not open by asking for a mental health history. The conversation can remain supportive while expectations and next steps stay clear.

tabs.label: Diagnosis first
tabs.body: Starting with a diagnosis makes an unsupported medical explanation the frame for the discussion. It can make the employee feel compelled to disclose or reject a label. Begin with the work evidence and route medical or support questions through the responsible process.

tabs.label: Work evidence
tabs.body: Work evidence helps the supervisor explain a concern and examine possible conditions. It does not require assuming there is no health issue. It creates a clear starting point from which an employee can raise a need and the supervisor can coordinate appropriately.

tabs.label: Avoidance
tabs.body: Avoiding all feedback may feel protective, but leaves the employee without a clear expectation or chance to respond. Respectful support includes explaining relevant work concerns. Choose a private, specific conversation rather than silence or an informal personal diagnosis.

check.question: What can the missed review dates establish?
check.correct: A specific work concern to discuss, without diagnosing its cause.
wrong: Proof of a mental health condition.
A conclusion that the employee is dangerous.
check.feedbackCorrect: The dates provide work evidence, while the cause and any support need remain to be clarified appropriately.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Missed dates may be concerning, but they do not establish diagnosis, danger, or permanent attitude. Those conclusions substitute stereotypes for evidence. Explain the work concern privately and invite discussion of relevant barriers and support within the supervisor’s role.

items.text: Two agreed review dates were missed.

Are the priorities and review instructions clear?
What work barriers need attention?

intro.heading: Recognize a request even when it uses ordinary words
intro.body:
An employee may say that a health condition makes concentration difficult and ask for written instructions, a change in schedule, or a quieter location. The employee does not have to use the phrase “reasonable accommodation” for the statement to need an appropriate response. A request begins a process; it does not automatically approve the requested option.

In the practice benefits team, an employee says that a medical condition makes rapid verbal instructions hard to follow and asks for a written summary. The supervisor should recognize the request and follow the agency’s accommodation procedures, including prompt forwarding to the appropriate decision maker. The supervisor should not leave it pending as an informal favor.

Explain what will happen next and who will provide updates. Do not require the employee to develop a complete solution before the request is considered. Under MMB Policy 1433, supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation from applicants or employees seeking accommodation. Any appropriate medical-information request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator; agencies must not request or accept medical records. Do not deny or delay forwarding because the request uses unfamiliar words.

items.title: Recognize
items.body: Identify the link between a requested work change and a medical condition. The statement about written instructions gives both. A general preference for written notes may be an ordinary work question; a health-related request needs appropriate coordination even if the employee does not know the policy name.

items.title: Forward
items.body: Policy 1433 directs the recipient to forward the request promptly to the appropriate decision maker and notify the requester who that is. Confirm the current agency route. In the team case, an unanswered note in a supervisor’s personal folder does not give the employee access to that process.

items.title: Clarify
items.body: Clarification concerns the work barrier and requested change, not a supervisor-led medical investigation. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation for accommodation under MMB Policy 1433. Any appropriate request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator, and medical records must not be requested or accepted. Promptly forward the request and explain the next-step contact.

tabs.label: Wait for terminology
tabs.body: Waiting for a policy phrase can appear orderly, but overlooks a request already communicated in ordinary language. It delays review for a reason unrelated to need. Respond to the substance and explain the established next step.

tabs.label: Recognize and route
tabs.body: Recognizing and routing the request preserves access to the appropriate decision process. It neither guarantees the requested arrangement nor treats it as optional kindness. Clear forwarding and updates help prevent a request from becoming invisible.

tabs.label: Immediate promise
tabs.body: Promising a particular arrangement can feel reassuring, but may exceed the supervisor’s authority or skip evaluation of effectiveness. Explain the process and coordinate any permitted immediate measures without presenting an unreviewed promise as the final decision.

check.question: What should the supervisor do with the health-related written-instruction request?
check.correct: Recognize it and follow the prompt agency forwarding and update process.
wrong: Personally require medical information or documentation before forwarding.
Promise final approval without checking authority.
check.feedbackCorrect: The ordinary-language statement raises a request, while the authorized process handles evaluation and decisions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Legal wording does not create the request; its substance does. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation for accommodation; any appropriate request belongs to the agency ADA Coordinator. An immediate approval promise may exceed authority. Recognize the request, forward it promptly and explain the responsible next step.

intro.heading: Offer support without replacing the appropriate process
intro.body:
Employee assistance can provide useful help with personal or workplace concerns. Leaders also have access to MMB Leadership and Team Dynamics consultation. These resources can support a person or a supervisor, but they do not make an accommodation decision, determine leave eligibility, or resolve a discrimination complaint in place of the responsible office.

An employee in the practice team asks for time to attend health appointments and also wants someone to talk with about stress. Those are related needs, but the response may involve both HR or accommodation coordination and current EAP information. Sending a counseling link alone leaves the employment request unanswered.

Offer accurate, current resource information and let the appropriate process explain its scope and privacy terms. Do not require an employee to report therapy details or prove EAP use as a condition of routine respect. If immediate help is needed, use urgent procedures and current crisis resources rather than relying on a routine referral email.

items.title: Support resource
items.body: A resource may help the employee work through concerns or help a leader manage a difficult team situation. MMB lists Leadership and Team Dynamics consultation for work-related mental-health concerns. Confirm current access details rather than copying an old provider name or assuming every benefit is identical.

items.title: Employment process
items.body: A schedule or leave question requires the relevant agency process. In the appointment case, HR can help identify applicable routes and responsibilities. The supervisor should not promise a leave entitlement, deny a work change, or assume a counseling referral answers the request.

items.title: Choice and privacy
items.body: Providing information is different from monitoring a person’s use of support. Ask what is needed for work coordination without requiring counseling details. If a separate formal referral or employment process applies, involve HR and explain it accurately rather than inventing conditions under the label of support.

tabs.label: Referral only
tabs.body: A referral is easy to offer and may be useful, but leaves a schedule or accommodation request unresolved if it is the only response. Identify what the employee is asking for and coordinate the employment question alongside support information.

tabs.label: Coordinated routes
tabs.body: Coordinated routes distinguish purposes and responsible people. This takes more attention than one link, but makes it clearer who handles leave, accommodation, or personal support. Do not require the employee to repeat unrelated personal details across every route.

tabs.label: Treatment monitoring
tabs.body: Monitoring counseling participation may seem to show follow-through. It shifts supervision into personal treatment information and does not establish job performance. Review appropriate work arrangements and use authorized processes rather than turning voluntary support use into a new work test.

check.question: What responds to both appointment scheduling and a wish for counseling support?
check.correct: Coordinate the employment request appropriately and offer current EAP information for the separate support need.
wrong: Send a counseling link and consider the schedule request closed.
Promise all requested leave without checking eligibility.
Require therapy details before discussing the schedule.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response addresses the different purposes without replacing formal decisions or collecting unrelated treatment information.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A counseling link can help but does not resolve a work schedule or leave request. A promise of leave can exceed authority, and therapy details are not needed for an initial work discussion. Identify the need, responsible route, and appropriate information for each purpose.

intro.heading: Protect privacy while keeping work coordination clear
intro.body:
When someone’s schedule or work arrangement changes, coworkers may have questions about coverage or fairness. They need relevant work information: who covers a task, what deadlines apply, and how assignments are made. They do not need an employee’s diagnosis, treatment, or accommodation records to understand those responsibilities.

In the practice team, coworkers ask why an employee has a revised schedule. The supervisor can explain the coverage plan and that individual arrangements are handled appropriately. Sharing a diagnosis to gain agreement creates exposure without resolving the team’s workload question.

Do not promise that information will never be shared with anyone. Authorized offices may need relevant information to address a request or another required process. Explain those limits respectfully, use approved channels, and avoid unnecessary details. Course reflections and team learning notes should not become informal health records.

lessons.keyStatement: Privacy and practical coordination can be maintained together.

items.title: Team explanation
items.body: Focus the team explanation on operations. For example, identify which employee covers the morning response queue and where urgent questions go. This gives coworkers what they need to perform their work without making a colleague’s health condition the public justification for a schedule.

items.title: Authorized sharing
items.body: Some information needs to reach HR or the ADA Coordinator for a legitimate purpose. Use the agency’s approved process and limit the content and recipients accordingly. Forwarding a request appropriately differs from copying a diagnosis into a team chat because coworkers are curious.

items.title: Privacy limits
items.body: A respectful conversation can explain that personal information will be handled through appropriate channels without promising absolute secrecy. If a required action is raised, consult the responsible office. An impossible promise may later damage trust more than a clear explanation of who needs what information and why.

tabs.label: Public justification
tabs.body: Publicly explaining a diagnosis may appear to settle questions about fairness. It places personal information before people who do not need it and can create new stereotypes. Answer the actual coverage or assignment question with work information instead.

tabs.label: Operational clarity
tabs.body: Operational clarity addresses the team’s real coordination needs. It does not invite staff to approve a colleague’s individual arrangement. Consistent expectations and an appropriate explanation of responsibilities can support confidence without exposing the reason for a private request.

tabs.label: Absolute secrecy
tabs.body: Absolute secrecy sounds reassuring but may conflict with responsibilities to route a request or respond to a serious concern. Explain privacy limits accurately. Keep disclosures purposeful and bounded instead of making a promise the supervisor cannot reliably honor.

check.question: How should the supervisor answer coworkers’ schedule questions?
check.correct: Explain coverage and work expectations without sharing personal health information.
wrong: Publish the employee’s diagnosis for fairness.
Share counseling details so the team understands.
Promise that no authorized office will ever receive relevant information.
check.feedbackCorrect: The operational explanation gives necessary clarity while personal information remains within its proper purpose.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A diagnosis or counseling history does not establish the coverage plan and is not needed for coworkers’ agreement. Absolute secrecy may prevent necessary coordination. Explain the work arrangement and handle relevant personal information through appropriate channels.

intro.heading: Keep safety response separate from stereotypes
intro.body:
An immediate safety or crisis situation needs timely help through established procedures. It should not wait for completion of a course, a routine consultant email, or a manager’s attempt to diagnose the person. Know the agency’s emergency procedures and current immediate-help resources before an urgent situation occurs. MMB’s leader resource lists 911 or 988 when help is needed right away.

This is different from deciding that a known mental health condition makes someone dangerous. Federal guidance requires objective evidence and an appropriate individualized assessment for employment decisions about a direct threat. A supervisor should not make that determination from gossip, a diagnosis, or a general fear.

In a team in this example, one situation involves a clear statement that immediate help is needed, while another involves rumors about a colleague receiving treatment. The first calls for the urgent route; the second does not justify excluding the colleague from work. Consult the responsible offices for safety and employment questions, and keep any record specific and appropriately protected.

lessons.keyStatement: Respond to the situation through the proper route, not a stereotype.

items.title: Immediate need
items.body: If immediate help is needed, follow the established emergency or crisis process. Do not use routine email as the main response. For example, a clear immediate-help statement requires timely coordination with the proper responders, not waiting until next week’s supervision meeting or completing a workplace analysis exercise.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: A direct-threat employment determination is an authorized, individualized question requiring appropriate objective evidence. A diagnosis or rumor is not that evidence. If a supervisor has a specific safety concern, describe the actual observation and seek the proper guidance rather than declaring a medical conclusion independently.

items.title: Preparation
items.body: Preparation means knowing routes and responsibilities before urgency arises. Confirm the agency procedure, who handles immediate situations, and how to obtain leadership consultation for non-immediate concerns. Avoid inventing a universal script or collecting employees’ diagnostic information to predict who might need help.

tabs.label: Routine work concern
tabs.body: A missed deadline or unclear instruction usually calls for work-focused discussion and appropriate support coordination. Do not escalate it into a medical safety conclusion without relevant evidence. Address the actual concern while preserving the ability to respond if an immediate issue emerges.

tabs.label: Urgent route
tabs.body: An urgent route is designed for immediate help and should be used promptly when the situation calls for it. It is separate from course reflection, routine EAP information, or a consultant appointment. Follow established procedures rather than improvising a clinical assessment.

tabs.label: Diagnosis-based exclusion
tabs.body: Excluding someone because of a diagnosis may feel precautionary, but substitutes a stereotype for a specific assessment. Employment decisions need appropriate evidence and authorized review. A known condition is not by itself a reason to remove development, public contact, or ordinary work.

check.question: Which statement is sound?
check.correct: Use urgent procedures when immediate help is needed, and do not treat diagnosis alone as proof of danger.
wrong: Routine email is enough for every immediate situation.
A supervisor should diagnose staff to predict emergencies.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response separates timely help from unsupported employment conclusions and stays within the proper responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Precaution does not justify a diagnosis-based prediction of danger. Routine email also cannot replace timely urgent procedures. Supervisors should know the established routes and present specific observations to responsible responders or offices rather than conduct their own clinical assessment.

items.text: Confirm the current agency emergency route.
Know how to obtain immediate help when needed.
Record the actual statement that prompted the response.
Describe the concrete incident to the responsible office.
Treatment means the person is dangerous.
A diagnosis list can forecast every crisis.

intro.heading: Follow through on work arrangements and recurring pressures
intro.body:
A supportive first conversation matters, but a request can still fail if it never reaches the right office or an approved arrangement is not implemented. Confirm the responsible next step and the appropriate update route. Follow-up should examine how the work arrangement functions, not require the employee to describe treatment or prove personal recovery.

In the practice benefits team, written instructions are agreed but disappear during a busy week. The supervisor can check delivery and clarity, coordinate an unresolved issue with the responsible process, and restore the arrangement as appropriate. Calling the employee uncooperative without checking implementation misses the work condition.

Also examine recurring pressures the leader can change: conflicting priorities, repeated last-minute requests, unsupported workload, or disrespectful communication. Better instructions may improve a work process without establishing a medical outcome. Use appropriate evidence and preserve formal routes for accommodation, leave, and workplace concerns. Support and relevant accountability can continue together.

inThisLesson: Plan an update that checks the work arrangement without probing treatment.
Identify a recurring team pressure that a leader can examine.

lessons.keyStatement: Support needs follow-through, and work design still needs review.

items.title: Implementation
items.body: Check that the agreed work arrangement actually occurred. If written instructions were not provided, an employee’s difficulty cannot be interpreted as if the arrangement had been delivered. Confirm responsibilities and coordinate the gap rather than assuming the employee failed to benefit from a support that never arrived.

items.title: Work conditions
items.body: Recurring pressure can come from how work is assigned and coordinated. In the benefits team, conflicting urgent tasks may require a management priority decision. Review that practice without collecting diagnoses or claiming that one work change explains every employee’s wellbeing.

items.title: Review
items.body: Use evidence proportionate to the question. Clearer instructions and fewer missed handoffs can show a process improvement. They do not prove recovery, establish treatment effectiveness, or resolve every legal responsibility. Record the improvement, remaining limitations, responsible follow-up, and any appropriate formal next step.

tabs.label: First conversation only
tabs.body: A kind first conversation is valuable but cannot demonstrate that the next step occurred. Without follow-through, the employee may still be waiting for a decision or arrangement. Confirm the route and responsibilities rather than treating empathy as completion.

tabs.label: Work-focused follow-up
tabs.body: Work-focused follow-up examines whether instructions, schedule, or support coordination functioned as intended. It can identify a repair without asking for treatment details. Keep individual support reviews private and route decisions through the appropriate offices.

tabs.label: Health outcome claim
tabs.body: A report that staff are now mentally healthy exceeds ordinary management evidence. Better work coordination may be encouraging without measuring clinical outcomes. Describe the actual process result and its limits instead of using personal wellbeing as an unsupported success metric.

check.question: What should follow-up on written instructions examine?
check.correct: Whether the agreed instructions were delivered and usable, with unresolved issues coordinated appropriately.
wrong: Whether the employee can prove counseling progress.
A claim that improved handoffs establish recovery.
Only whether the first conversation felt supportive.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review tests implementation and work usability while leaving health and treatment questions in their proper place.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Counseling progress and medical recovery are not the supervisor’s routine process measures. A positive first conversation also does not show that instructions were delivered. Check the work arrangement, coordination, and remaining issues without requiring treatment details.

Did the request reach the identified decision maker?

move.failure: An undelivered arrangement is judged ineffective or a small improvement becomes a health claim.
move.next: Choose an implementation question, a work-condition improvement, and a responsible follow-up date.

jobAid.subtitle: Describe the work, listen respectfully, choose the right route, and check follow-through.
remember: A work concern is not a diagnosis.
A support referral does not replace a formal employment process.
Share personal information only for the appropriate authorized purpose.

sections.heading: A respectful conversation
items: State the observed work concern and expectation.
Describe the work barrier and requested change; do not personally request medical information or documentation for accommodation.
Explain limits on privacy and the next appropriate step.

sections.heading: Choose the route
items: Coordinate possible accommodation requests with the responsible agency process.
Route leave and employment questions to HR rather than making promises.
Offer current EAP information and use immediate-help procedures when needed.

sections.heading: Follow through
items: Confirm that the request reached the appropriate decision maker.
Check the work arrangement without probing treatment details.
Review recurring work pressures and protect opportunity from stereotypes.

sources.title: EEOC — Mental Health Conditions in the Workplace: Your Legal Rights
sources.note: Primary federal guidance on discrimination, privacy, accommodation, and evidence-based decisions. The course does not determine an individual’s legal eligibility.

sources.title: MMB — ADA Reasonable Accommodation Policy 1433
sources.note: State policy describing ordinary-language requests, prompt forwarding, the interactive process, responsibilities, and confidentiality. Confirm current agency procedures for actual work.

sources.title: MMB — Leadership and Team Dynamics
sources.note: Current state resource for leaders’ consultation through the EAP, including mental-health workplace concerns. Lists immediate-help routes; this course is not a crisis-response protocol.
